issues.feedback: Marker handling is incomplete: clamping only when `marker_loop < checkpoint_loop` misses rollback-to-same-loop cases. If checkpoint is loop N in a non-planning phase and user rolls back to N, reconstruction can still resume non-planning. Marker should also force planning when `checkpoint_loop == marker_loop`.

The spec does not define behavior for invalid/corrupt `.rollback-target` contents (non-integer, negative, empty). Reconstruction should treat malformed markers as non-fatal (ignore + warn), otherwise commands like `status`/`project show` can fail unexpectedly.

`original_head` capture order is ambiguous. If captured before checking out the project branch, push-failure recovery can reset the project branch to the wrong commit. The spec should require capturing rollback anchor after switching to the target project branch (or capturing both branch+HEAD explicitly).

Fallback behavior is underspecified at the CLI contract level: after reverting local HEAD and applying soft rollback, should command exit success or non-zero? Acceptance criteria should explicitly require exit code and user-facing message so callers can rely on deterministic behavior.

Clearing marker in `checkpoint_phase_transition` is directionally correct, but timing is unspecified. If marker is deleted before commit/push succeeds, a failed checkpoint can lose rollback intent and re-expose stale checkpoints. Marker must be removed only after successful checkpoint commit+push.

Current rollback logic only checks out project branch if it exists locally; otherwise reset runs on current branch. The spec does not address this hazard. Hard rollback should fail fast (or create/sync and checkout project branch) before any destructive reset.

Test plan is mostly unit/integration-oriented, but this repo requires validate conformance coverage for CLI behavior. The spec should include concrete `src/validate/` tests for soft rollback (no git mutation), hard rollback, push-failure recovery path, dry-run messaging, and marker lifecycle/cleanup.
